rationale: A wins because it keeps the weak spots in plain view instead of polishing them into fake certainty. Its line, "no satellite in orbit yet" is a feature of the story rather than a hole, turns the biggest liability into a real VC question. B has teeth, especially "A state fire agency signed an MOU with a satellite startup that hasn't launched anything," but then it steps on the rake with "pre-revenue, pre-launch hardware" and "engineers" when the update only says revenue is undisclosed and the founders are alumni.
gaps_in_A: "launch-hardware discipline from one company, Earth-observation operations from the other" assumes the founders worked in those functions; the update only gives employer lineage.

"The founder-profile angle needs the least missing proof and can go first" is a little too easy. Ex-SpaceX/Planet alumni are not automatically a story unless their actual roles, seniority, or operating scars are worth printing.
gaps_in_B: "Ex-SpaceX and Planet Labs engineers" invents roles. The update says founders are ex-SpaceX and ex-Planet Labs, not engineers.
"checks written against pre-revenue, pre-launch hardware" invents pre-revenue status. Revenue is not disclosed; that is not the same as zero.
"says something about how desperate agencies are for faster detection, or how loose tech MOUs have become" turns one unnamed MOU into a trend thesis without evidence.
"June sits inside the Northern Hemisphere fire season" is calendar color, not a supplied news signal. It is handled carefully, but it is still a soft peg trying to dress up a funding announcement.
